headline: Running 100B+ MoE Models on a Single RTX 4090: A Practical Guide to Expert Offloading with llama.cpp
summary: A new guide details how to run 100B+ Mixture of Experts (MoE) models on an NVIDIA RTX 4090's 24GB VRAM. This is achieved through expert offloading, leveraging system RAM for less active model components.
details: A recent guide demonstrates how to run 125B parameter Mixture of Experts (MoE) models on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090, which typically has only 24GB of VRAM. This is remarkable, as a 125B model quantized to 4-bit usually requires 70-75GB of memory.

The secret lies in the MoE architecture itself and a technique called expert offloading. Unlike dense models where every token passes through all parameters, MoE models only activate a few 'experts' per layer for each token.

This means a 125B MoE model might only have 10-15B active parameters per token. The core idea is to keep the continuously used parts, like the KV cache and attention, on the GPU, while offloading the larger, less frequently accessed expert layers to system RAM.

The CPU then only needs to process a small number of selected experts per token, maintaining acceptable speeds. Crucially, RAM bandwidth becomes more important than CPU core count for performance in this setup.

For optimal performance, using two large-capacity RAM sticks is often better than four smaller ones on consumer platforms, as it helps maintain higher bus speeds. Proper CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES settings, like '89' for Ada (RTX 4090), also optimize build times.

When selecting model files, prioritize pre-quantized GGUF versions, especially dynamic or imatrix quantizations like Q4_K_M or IQ4_XS. For MoE models, IQ4_XS often provides near Q4_K_M quality with 10-15% less RAM usage.

Configuration can be done simply with `--n-cpu-moe N` to keep the first N layers on the CPU, or with `-ot` (override-tensor) for precise tensor placement. The tuning process involves gradually reducing N while monitoring VRAM with `nvidia-smi` to leave 1-2GB headroom.

It's important to benchmark performance using tools like `llama-bench` and custom API scripts, as real-world speeds vary significantly based on RAM, context length, and quantization type. Focus on Time To First Token (TTFT) and decode tokens per second.

For long prompts or RAG use cases, prefill speed can be a bottleneck due to CPU-bound expert calculations. Increasing batch size (`-b` and `-ub`, e.g., `-ub 2048`) can help `llama.cpp` offload prefill expert computations more efficiently to the GPU.

Expert offloading transforms the challenge of running large models from requiring expensive multi-GPU clusters to needing a mid-range GPU and ample, cheaper DDR5 system RAM. This approach is highly valuable for developers needing to run large models locally while keeping sensitive data secure.

headline_marked: [[Stop AI labelling your Photoshop and Premiere exports]] on Instagram & TikTok
headline: Stop AI labelling your Photoshop and Premiere exports on Instagram & TikTok
summary: Generative edits in Photoshop and Premiere Pro embed Content Credentials (C2PA) that social media platforms read, leading to automatic AI labels. Export settings don't disable them.
details: When using generative AI features like Generative Fill in Photoshop or Generative Extend in Premiere Pro, your exported files automatically carry Content Credentials (C2PA). These digital markers are read by platforms like Instagram, Facebook, TikTok, YouTube, and LinkedIn, which then apply an "AI info" label to your content.

Crucially, standard export settings in Adobe applications do not offer an option to disable these embedded Content Credentials. This means that any file that has undergone even a minor generative edit will be flagged as AI-generated upon upload to social media.

For content creators and professionals, this can be a significant workflow interruption. The article provides solutions, including a free script for manual checking and removal, and a dedicated application called MetaClean for automated processing on Mac and Windows.

MetaClean offers a "Watch Folders" feature that runs in the background, monitoring export directories for new JPG, PNG, MP4, or MOV files. It automatically detects Content Credentials or AI-origin tags, then creates a verified clean copy of the file without re-encoding, preserving color profiles and orientation. It also includes a batch mode for existing archives and costs $5 after a 3-day free trial.
